Dear Ms. Reese:

Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC (“Columbia Gulf”) hereby files pursuant to and in
accordance with Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, 1 and Part 157, Subpart A of the Federal
Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) regulations, 2 an abbreviated
application (“Application”) for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity requesting
authorization of its Clark Project (“Project”), located in Estill and Clark counties, Kentucky.

The proposed Project involves the construction of approximately 8.68 miles of 30-inch diameter
pipeline, one new point of delivery, and associated facilities. Once completed, the Project
facilities will provide up to 250,000 dekatherms per day (“Dth/d”) of firm transportation capacity
to the Project Shipper, helping ensure a reliable and cost-effective energy supply for Kentucky
consumers. The Project will also enhance the reliability and flexibility of the regional power
grid, support growing energy demand, and contribute to continued economic development in the
region.

Columbia Gulf respectfully requests Commission approval of the Project on or before August,
2027, to ensure sufficient time for Columbia Gulf to safely construct and complete the Project.
Timely approval will allow Columbia Gulf to meet the targeted in-service date of August 1,
2028, and fulfill its commitment to delivering reliable energy infrastructure in support of market
demand.

Columbia Gulf is e-filing this Application in accordance with the Commission’s Order No. 703
Filing Via the Internet guidelines issued in Docket No. RM07-16-000 on November 15, 2007.
The instant filing is comprised of four (4) volumes containing Public, Privileged and CEII
material as detailed below:

placed on the Internet as “Public Information”. Any information contained in the Public Volumes
that is considered privileged and confidential or CEII has been removed, and such instances are
identified within the Public Volume.

Columbia Gulf requests that information submitted in Volume III and marked as both
“CUI//PRIV” and “Contains Privileged and Confidential Information - Do Not Release” be
accorded privileged and confidential treatment pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 388.112 of the
Commission’s regulations. The documents in that volume contain sensitive data, proprietary
information, or information that otherwise is not appropriate for disclosure to the public.

Pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 388.113 of the Commission’s regulations, Columbia Gulf has submitted
Volume IV as “CUI//CEII - Contains Critical Energy Infrastructure Information – Do Not
Release”. Columbia Gulf is submitting this volume as CEII because it contains information
about the proposed critical infrastructure that could be useful to a person planning an attack on
its pipeline and aboveground facilities. Columbia Gulf requests that this information be treated as
CEII for as long as the subject facilities are in service.

Additionally, Columbia Gulf herein submits its hydraulic models (“Models”) supporting Exhibits
G, G-I and G-II to the Application for the Project. Columbia Gulf is submitting these Models
pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 388.113 of the Commission’s regulations. The information contained in
these Models contains specific engineering, vulnerability, and detailed information about
proposed and existing infrastructure that (i) relates details about the transportation of natural gas;
(ii) could be useful to a person in planning an attack on critical infrastructure; (iii) is exempt
from mandatory disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. 552; and (iv) does
not simply give the general location of the critical infrastructure.

Consequently, the Models have been marked as “CUI//PRIV//CEII Confidential,

           FOR A CERTIFICATE OF PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECCESSITY

           Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC ("Columbia Gulf"), pursuant to and in accordance with

Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”), as amended, 1 and Part 157 of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) regulations, 2 hereby files this abbreviated

application (“Application”) requesting authorization to construct, own, and operate the Clark

Project (“Project”) in Estill and Clark Counties, Kentucky. The proposed Project, as discussed

further herein, involves the construction of approximately 8.68 miles of new 30-inch diameter

pipeline, one new point of delivery (“POD”), and associated facilities. Once completed, the Project

facilities will provide up to 250,000 dekatherms per day (“Dth/d”) of firm transportation capacity

to the Project Shipper, helping ensure a reliable and cost-effective energy supply for Kentucky

consumers. The Project will also enhance the reliability and flexibility of the regional power grid,

support growing energy demand, and contribute to continued economic development in the region.

           Columbia Gulf has executed a binding precedent agreement with East Kentucky Power

Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC” or “Project Shipper”) for 100% of the Project’s transportation capacity

of 250,000 Dth/d for a term of 20 years, commencing August 1, 2028. This executed precedent

agreement provides substantial evidence of market demand for the proposed transportation service

and for the facilities requested herein. The Project has been designed to provide the requested


1

2
    18 C.F.R. § 157 (2026).
 service efficiently, while minimizing impacts on existing customers, landowners, surrounding

communities, and environmental resources.

           To meet the timeline requested by the Project Shipper and to ensure the safe and efficient

construction of the proposed facilities, Columbia Gulf respectfully requests that the Commission

issue an order granting the authorizations requested herein on or before August 2027. Timely

issuance of the order will enable Columbia Gulf to commence construction in alignment with the

Project schedule and support an August 1, 2028, contractual in-service date, as outlined in the

precedent agreement with the Project Shipper.

           In support of this Application, Columbia Gulf is submitting the following materials, which

collectively demonstrate the Project’s market justification, technical feasibility, environmental

compatibility, and alignment with the public convenience and necessity standard under the NGA.

                                                  I.
                        INFORMATION REGARDING THE APPLICANT

           The applicant’s exact legal name is Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC. Columbia Gulf is

a limited liability company organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware with its

principal place of business located at 700 Louisiana Street, Suite 1300, Houston, Texas 77002-

2700, and is indirectly owned by TransCanada Pipeline USA Ltd. and Global Infrastructure

Partners. Columbia Gulf is a “natural-gas company” as defined under the NGA, 3 engaged

primarily in the business of transporting natural gas and operating underground storage fields in

interstate commerce under authorizations granted by and subject to the jurisdiction of the

Commission. Columbia Gulf is authorized to do business in the states of Delaware, Kentucky,

Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Texas, West Virginia and Wyoming.

                                               II.
                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The Clark Project was developed in direct response to EKPC’s request for long-term firm

natural gas transportation capacity to serve its existing J.K. Smith Station, a 1,055-megawatt peak-

load electric generation facility (“Smith Station”) located in Clark County, Kentucky (“Clark

Project”). The Smith Station provides important electric generation and voltage support for the

Kentucky electric grid. To meet its firm transportation requirements, EKPC executed a binding

precedent agreement with Columbia Gulf for 250,000 Dth/d of firm transportation service for a

twenty-year term.

       Upon completion, the Clark Project will provide the transportation infrastructure necessary

to serve the Smith Station and satisfy EKPC’s identified need for reliable, long-term transportation

capacity. By expanding the state’s natural gas infrastructure, the Clark Project will serve as key



                                                 3
 infrastructure that will strengthen the reliability and flexibility of Kentucky’s power grid, support

regional economic development and growing demands on its system, including the growing

demands of Kentucky’s power-generation customers.

        To gauge broader market interest in the Clark Project beyond the commitment from EKPC,

Columbia Gulf conducted a binding open season in accordance with Section 4.2(a) of the General

Terms and Conditions (“GT&C”) of its FERC Gas Tariff, Third Revised Volume No. 1, as

amended (“Tariff”). The binding open season was held from September 14 through September 18,

2026, offering firm transportation service for all capacity to be made available by the Project. At

the conclusion of the open season, Columbia Gulf received no other competing bids, and Columbia

Gulf entered into a 20-year precedent agreement with EKPC for 100% of the 250,000 Dth/d of

capacity. The result of the open season confirms strong market support for the Project and

demonstrates EKPC’s commitment to securing reliable, long-term transportation capacity.

        The Project satisfies the Commission’s Certificate Policy Statement 4 because it is fully

supported by long-term binding precedent agreements for 100% of the proposed capacity,

demonstrating clear market demand for the requested facilities. The Project will not result in

subsidization by existing customers, will not adversely affect service to existing customers or other

pipelines and their customers, and has been designed to avoid or minimize impacts on landowners,

surrounding communities, and environmental resources to the maximum extent practicable.

        As demonstrated throughout this Application and the accompanying Environmental

Report, the Project is required by the public convenience and necessity. The Project will provide

the firm transportation capacity necessary to meet the Project Shipper’s identified needs while



4

                                                      4
 maintaining reliable service to Columbia Gulf’s existing customers. In addition to meeting the

energy needs of the Project Shipper, the proposed Project is expected to generate positive

economic impacts across the region. These include the creation of new job opportunities during

the construction phase, increased labor income, and a boost in local spending. The Project will

also generate additional tax revenues that can support state and local priorities such as

infrastructure, education, and public services. Through ongoing stakeholder engagement and

careful project planning, Columbia Gulf and EKPC are working together to deliver critical energy

infrastructure that supports both regional economic growth and community priorities.

       To meet the timing requested by the Project Shipper, and to ensure the safe and efficient

construction of proposed facilities, Columbia Gulf respectfully requests that the Commission issue

an order granting the authorizations requested herein by August 2027.

Resource Report 1, General Project Description, provided as part of the Environmental Report and

attached as Exhibit F-1 to this Application:

       The specific descriptions and locations of the proposed Project facilities, including

drawings that outline both the permanent and temporary workspaces required for the Project, are

set forth in Resource Report 1 contained in Exhibit F-1 attached to this Application. Flow diagrams

and data demonstrating the effect of the proposed Project on the operational capabilities and

conditions of Columbia Gulf’s system are included herein as Exhibits G, G-I, and G-II. These flow

diagrams also demonstrate that there will be no adverse impact to service provided to Columbia

Gulf’s existing customers as a result of this Project.

Reservation of Capacity

       Pursuant to Section 4.2(b) of the GT&C of Columbia Gulf’s Tariff, Columbia Gulf has

reserved 250,000 Dth/d of unsubscribed firm transportation capacity on its system to support the

Project. This reserved capacity originates from Columbia Gulf’s Mainline Pool to the newly

established point of delivery to be constructed as part of the Project. By utilizing existing

unsubscribed capacity, Columbia Gulf is able to minimize the scope of new facilities required for

the Project. This strategic use of available system capacity allows Columbia Gulf to extend its

mainline facilities to deliver the requested capacity to the Smith Station.



                                                  6
            This approach not only meets the market need of the Project Shipper efficiently and cost-

effectively but also helps to reduce environmental impacts and limit construction-related

disruptions.

Project Cost

           The total estimated cost of the Project is $95 million, which includes the Allowance for

Funds Used During Construction (“AFUDC”). A detailed breakdown of the estimated capital

expenditures associated with the Project is provided in Exhibit K attached to this Application.

These estimates reflect Columbia Gulf’s current engineering, procurement, and construction

planning and are based on industry-standard cost assumptions and methodologies.

AFUDC

           Columbia Gulf represents that the AFUDC accruals included in the total Project cost, as set

forth in Exhibit K, are consistent with the Commission’s policy on AFUDC accounting, as outlined

in Docket No. AD10-3-000. 5 Columbia Gulf confirms that it has incurred capital expenditures related

to the Project and that activities necessary to prepare the Project for its intended use were underway

at the time AFUDC accruals commenced. These activities include engineering design, environmental

permitting, land acquisition, and other pre-construction efforts. Columbia Gulf will continue to apply

AFUDC in accordance with the Commission’s guidelines and accounting standards, ensuring

transparency and regulatory compliance throughout the development and construction phases of the

Project.

                                                     IV.
                                        MARKET SUPPORT

        The incremental capacity created by the Clark Project is a market driven response to a

direct request from EKPC for long-term firm natural gas transportation service to support its

existing Smith Station located in Clark County, Kentucky. Once in service, the Clark Project will

provide the transportation infrastructure necessary to deliver natural gas to EKPC’s Smith Station

and support the reliability and flexibility of electric generation resources available to meet the

state’s growing energy needs.

        The Commission has consistently recognized that precedent agreements for long-term firm

transportation service constitute persuasive evidence of market need. 6 Accordingly, the executed

precedent agreements supporting the Project provide substantial evidence of demand for the

proposed facilities and demonstrate that the Project is required to satisfy the transportation

requirements identified by the Project Shippers. A copy of the executed precedent agreement is

included in Exhibit I to this application.

        EKPC is a not-for-profit generation and transmission electric utility headquartered in

Winchester, Kentucky, that provides electric generation capacity and electric energy to sixteen

owner-member cooperatives, which in turn serve approximately 1.2 million Kentuckians across

eighty-nine counties in Kentucky. 7           EKPC’s Smith Station is an existing 1,055-megawatt

generating facility that provides peaking capacity during periods of high electrical demand and

supports reliable operation of Kentucky’s electric grid.

(quoting Sierra Club v. FERC, 153 F.4th 1295, 1309 (D.C. Circ. 2025)).

                                                       8
         To further assess market interest, Columbia Gulf conducted a binding open season in

accordance with Section 4.2 of the GT&C of its Tariff from September 14 to September 18, 2026.

Columbia Gulf offered firm transportation service for all capacity to be made available by the

Project. At the conclusion of the open season, no other bids were received, and Columbia Gulf

entered into a 20-year precedent agreement with EKPC for 100% of the 250,000 Dth/d created by

the Project. In addition, Columbia Gulf also offered to evaluate proposals from existing shippers

to turn back firm transportation capacity under existing service agreements. Columbia Gulf

received no offers for turnback capacity.

        In summary, Columbia Gulf’s proposal is supported by demonstrated market demand and

satisfies the needs expressed by EKPC in the binding precedent agreement that has been executed

for the Project. By increasing natural gas delivery capabilities, the Project strengthens access to

affordable and reliable energy, strengthen Kentucky’s electric grid, and support continued

economic development throughout the region.

                                                    V.
                               COST RECOVERY AND TARIFF

        The proposed firm transportation service associated with the Project will be provided under

Columbia Gulf’s existing Rate Schedule FTS-1 and in accordance with Part 284, Subpart G of the

Commission’s regulations. Columbia Gulf requests predetermination of rolled-in rate treatment

for the costs and revenues associated with the Project, in accordance with the Commission’s

Certificate Policy Statement 8. As described in the Policy Statement, rolled-in rate treatment is

appropriate when revenues exceed estimated cost-of-service. To support a request for a



8
 Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas Pipeline Facilities, Statement of Policy, 88 FERC ¶ 61,227 (1999);
Order Clarifying Statement of Policy, 90 FERC ¶ 61,128 (2000); Order Further Clarifying Statement of Policy, 92
FERC ¶ 61,094 (2000) (“Policy Statement”).



                                                      9
 predetermination that a pipeline may roll the costs of a project into its system-wide rates in its next

NGA Section 4 rate proceeding, a pipeline must demonstrate that rolling-in the costs associated

with the proposal will not result in existing customers subsidizing the Project.

       The estimated cost-of-service and revenues of the Project are reflected in Exhibit N and

are based on cost-of-service factors approved by the Commission in Docket Nos. RP97-502 and

RP23-887. The proposed Project will generate an estimated three-year average cost-of-service of

$12.8 million while the revenues will average $19.1 million. Based on the estimated cost-of-

service and revenues of the Project, Columbia Gulf has demonstrated that the Project will not result

in subsidization by existing customers, and therefore, the Commission should grant a

predetermination of rolled-in rate treatment. Accordingly, Columbia Gulf proposed to apply the

existing FTS-1 base system recourse reservation and commodity rates for the Project.

       Consistent with Commission policy, Columbia Gulf will maintain a separate record of

capital costs for the Project facilities in its books and accounts. Moreover, Columbia Gulf will

maintain separate and identifiable accounts for the billing determinants, operating expenses, and

revenues associated with the Project in sufficient detail so that they can be identified in Statements

G, I, and J in any future NGA Section 4 rate case. For the reasons described herein, Columbia Gulf

respectfully requests that the Commission make a preliminary determination that, absent a

significant change in circumstances, the Project facilities will be rolled-in to Columbia Gulf’s

existing base-system rates in Columbia Gulf’s future NGA Section 4 rate proceeding.

       In addition to the request for predetermination of roll-in, the Project Shipper has agreed to

pay a negotiated recourse rate for the firm transportation service, as set forth in the Negotiated

Rate Letter Agreement between Columbia Gulf and the Project Shipper. Columbia Gulf will

provide this service in accordance with the negotiated rate authority set forth in Section 34 of the




                                                  10
 GT&C of its Tariff. As provided for in the Commission’s Negotiated Rate Policy Statement,

Columbia Gulf will file the associated negotiated rate agreement with the Commission 30 to 60

days prior to the date the underlying negotiated rates are proposed to become effective.

       Columbia Gulf does not anticipate the construction of any new compression facilities as

part of the Project, nor an increase in fuel consumption expected at existing compressor stations.

In fact, Columbia Gulf expects the Project to reduce its generally applicable system fuel retention

rate, as it will increase throughput in a south-to-north direction and will not include incremental

fuel usage, ultimately benefiting existing customers. Accordingly, Columbia Gulf proposes to

apply its generally applicable system fuel retention rate to the Project capacity. Furthermore, the

Project shipper has agreed to pay Company Use fuel in accordance with the terms outlined in the

executed Precedent Agreement.

                                                 VI.
                              ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS

       Columbia Gulf has designed the Project with a strong commitment to environmental

stewardship, incorporating measures to avoid, minimize, and mitigate potential impacts to the

greatest extent practicable, as further detailed in the Environmental Report (Exhibit F-1). This

report includes Resource Reports 1-12, prepared in accordance with 18 C.F.R. Part 380 of the

Commission's regulations, and the Commission’s Guidance Manual for Environmental Report

Preparation. The Environmental Report outlines Columbia Gulf’s use of proven construction

techniques and best management practices to protect sensitive environmental resources. The

Project is designed to avoid or minimize impacts on landowners, streams, wetlands, threatened

and endangered species, cultural resources and historic resources, and recreational or scenic areas.

Exhibit J – Federal Authorizations, provides a listing of all federal permits, licenses, approvals, or

authorizations that are required for the proposed Project.


                                                 11
          Columbia Gulf’s analysis in the Environmental Report demonstrates that potential impacts

can be effectively avoided or mitigated through site-specific planning and implementation of

environmental controls. The proposed action represents the best alternative to meet the Project’s

purpose and need, balancing environmental, technical, and economic considerations.

Compensatory mitigation and restoration will ensure that no significant resources will be

irreversibly or irretrievably lost. Based on this analysis, Columbia Gulf respectfully submits that

the Project does not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality of the

human environment and therefore qualifies for a Finding of No Significant Impact.

         Columbia Gulf will construct the Project in full compliance with all applicable federal,

state, and local environmental permits and approvals. 9 The Project-specific plans and

specifications incorporate key Commission requirements, including erosion and sedimentation

control, revegetation and restoration, and wetland and waterbody protection measures. Columbia

Gulf will employ at least one environmental inspector during construction to ensure compliance

with applicable environmental conditions and permit requirements. These inspectors will have the

authority to stop work if necessary to prevent environmental harm.

         Columbia Gulf is committed to minimizing disruption to nearby communities and

ecosystems. Construction activities are not anticipated to result in significant adverse effects on

residential or industrial areas, public health and safety, wildlife and vegetation, streams or

wetlands, or cultural and recreational resources. Columbia Gulf will reclaim all disturbed areas to

a consistently high standard, regardless of ownership, and will continue to engage with

stakeholders to ensure transparency and responsiveness throughout the construction and

restoration process. For the reasons outlined above and detailed in the accompanying


9
 Exhibit J – Federal Authorizations, included herein, provides a listing of all federal permits, licenses, approvals, or
authorizations that are required for the proposed Project.


                                                          12
 Environmental Report, Columbia Gulf respectfully requests that the Commission find that the

Project will not result in significant environmental impacts and that approval under Section 7 of

the NGA is warranted.

                                                 VII.
              LANDOWNER NOTIFICATION AND PROJECT OUTREACH

       Columbia Gulf has undertaken a robust and proactive outreach program to engage

landowners, elected officials, and other stakeholders regarding the proposed Project. A central

objective of Columbia Gulf’s outreach strategy is to foster transparent, timely, and respectful

communication with all parties potentially affected by the Project. Outreach efforts formally began

in March 2025 with the distribution of letters requesting survey permission. Building on this initial

engagement, Columbia Gulf will send invitations in late-October 2026, for public open houses to

be held on November 10, 2026, in the City of Winchester, Kentucky. Invitations will be extended

to a range of stakeholders, including local, state and federal government officials, as well as

federally recognized and state-recognized tribes. Each invitation includes a description of the

Project, a fact sheet including the location of the proposed facilities, and the Project website, which

went live on October 19, 2026. Open house ads will be placed in local newspapers in the weeks

prior to the event, ensuring interested community members have the opportunity to attend.

       Columbia Gulf will continue to distribute additional Project information to attendees,

landowners, and interested parties to ensure continued transparency and responsiveness to

questions received. Columbia Gulf remains committed to maintaining open lines of

communication throughout the life of the Project and sharing information on the Project’s progress

and potential impacts.

       In accordance with the landowner notification requirements set forth in 18 C.F.R. §

157.6(d) of the Commission’s regulations, Columbia Gulf will notify all owners of properties


                                                  13
 directly affected by the proposed construction activities, those abutting the proposed construction

areas, and any other landowners that may be directly impacted. A complete list of affected

landowners is provided under separate cover as Appendix 1F to Resource Report 1 and marked

“CUI//PRIV” and “Privileged and Confidential – Do Not Release” in accordance with the

Commission’s regulations.

                                            VIII.
                      PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY

       Columbia Gulf’s proposed Project is required by the present and future public convenience

and necessity. As demonstrated herein, the Project satisfies the criteria of the NGA, Part 157 of the

Commission’s regulations, and the Commission’s Certificate Policy Statement. The Project is

designed to serve EKPC’s Smith Station and satisfy EKPC’s identified need for reliable, long-term

transportation capacity, while ensuring that existing customers, competing pipelines, landowners,

or surrounding communities are not adversely impacted.

   A. No Subsidization by Existing Customers

       The Project is fully supported by a binding precedent agreement executed between

Columbia Gulf and the Project Shipper, which commits to 100% of the Project capacity of 250,000

Dth/d for a 20-year term. As reflected in Exhibit N, the Project revenues exceed the Project costs,

therefore, existing customers will not subsidize the costs of the new service. In addition, Columbia

Gulf expects the Project to reduce its generally applicable system fuel retention rate because the

Project will increase throughput in a south-to-north direction without requiring incremental fuel

usage, thereby providing an additional benefit to existing customers. Accordingly, the Project will

not result in the subsidization of facility costs by existing shippers and satisfies the Certificate

Policy Statement’s threshold requirement of no financial subsidies from existing shippers.




                                                 14
     B. Columbia Gulf Has Eliminated or Minimized and Will Continue to Eliminate or
       Minimize Potential Adverse Effects on Relevant Interests

        1. No Adverse Impact on Existing Customers

        The Project will not adversely affect Columbia Gulf’s existing customers or the services

they receive. The Project is designed to provide 100% of the proposed firm transportation capacity

of 250,000 Dth/d to service EKPC’s Smith Plant. As discussed above, the Project revenues exceed

the Project costs, and no changes are being proposed to Columbia Gulf’s existing Tariff provisions

or to its existing general applicable transportation rates, thereby ensuring that existing shippers

will not be adversely impacted. Additionally, Columbia Gulf expects the Project to reduce its

generally applicable system fuel retention rate, as it will increase throughput without adding

incremental fuel usage - ultimately benefiting existing customers.

        To demonstrate the Project’s compatibility with existing operations, Columbia Gulf has

included flow diagrams and supporting data in Exhibits G and G-II of this Application. These

exhibits confirm that the proposed facilities will not adversely impact the operational capabilities

of Columbia Gulf’s system or the quality of service provided to existing customers.

        Accordingly, there will be no adverse impacts to Columbia Gulf’s existing customers or

their contracted services as a result of the Project.

        2. No Adverse Impact on Other Pipelines or Their Customers

        The construction and operation of the Project will not adversely affect other existing

pipelines or their captive customers. The Project is designed to provide firm transportation service

to meet EKPC’s identified requirements and is not intended to replace firm service provided by

another pipeline. Instead, it is designed to support EKPC’s overall resource strategy and enhance

grid reliability in Kentucky. Any potential competitive effects are outweighed by the demonstrated

market need for the Project, the public benefits associated with the proposed facilities, and the



                                                  15
 Commission's long-standing policy favoring fair competition and increased access to natural gas

transportation services. Accordingly, the Project satisfies this element of the Certificate Policy

Statement, demonstrating that it will not result in adverse impacts on other pipelines or their

customers.

       3.    Interest of landowners and surrounding communities

       The proposed Project has been designed to avoid adverse impacts to landowners and the

surrounding communities. Columbia Gulf has prioritized minimizing disruptions by leveraging its

existing infrastructure, capacity, and footprint wherever feasible. As described in Section VII of

this Application, Columbia Gulf has actively engaged with landowners and community stakeholders

throughout the development process to identify concerns and incorporate refinements that reduce

environmental and land use impacts.

       While the Commission has recognized that pipeline construction projects will cause some

short-term impacts to landowners, Columbia Gulf designed the Project to mitigate these effects.

This includes adjusting the Project footprint to avoid sensitive areas and reduce potential

disturbances to landowners and the environment.

       To facilitate early and transparent engagement, Columbia Gulf initiated outreach efforts

with local landowners in March 2025, followed by engagement with federal, state, and local

elected officials beginning in April 2025. Columbia Gulf has contacted state legislators, county

and municipal officials, and members of the U.S. Senate and congressional delegation members

and/or their staff to apprise them of the Project.

       Columbia Gulf will host an in-person open house on November 10, 2026, in the City of

Winchester, Kentucky to provide information, answer questions, and gather additional feedback

from the public. To further facilitate stakeholder communication, Columbia Gulf established a




                                                     16
 public website for the Project at www.tcenergy.com/Clark which went live on October 19, 2026.

Columbia Gulf         remains       committed         to      ongoing      collaboration with all

affected landowners and stakeholders to address concerns and to minimize impacts throughout

development, construction, and operation of the Project facilities.

       Beyond its operational benefits, the Project is expected to generate positive economic

impacts across the region, including construction-related employment, labor income, increased tax

revenues, and associated economic activity. These benefits will support local and regional

economies while contributing to the continued development of energy infrastructure necessary to

meet Project Shippers’ requirements.

       Columbia Gulf submits that the selected location for the Project facilities represents the

environmentally preferable alternative, as more fully described in Exhibit F-1, Resource Report

No. 10. A detailed listing of the agencies and stakeholders consulted, as well as the applicable

permits and approvals, is provided in Exhibit F-1, Resource Report No. 1, and Exhibit J.

       Accordingly, Columbia Gulf submits that the Project satisfies this element of the

Commission's Certificate Policy Statement.

   C. Public Benefits Outweigh any Potential Adverse Effects

       Columbia Gulf has carefully designed the Project to avoid adverse impacts on landowners,

communities, and the environment. Although it is not possible to eliminate all impacts with

construction and operation of the Project, Columbia Gulf has implemented and will continue to

implement mitigation measures to reduce any residual effects to the maximum extent practicable.

       The Project will provide 250,000 Dth/d of firm transportation service to support EKPC's

electric generation requirements, strengthen the reliability and flexibility of Kentucky's power

grid, and help ensure that growing demand for electricity can be met through a reliable supply of



                                                17
 natural gas. The Project also is expected to generate temporary economic activity during

construction and contribute additional tax revenues to state and local governments.

        Importantly, the Project will not result in significant adverse effects on any population

within the Project area, nor will it displace permanent residents or businesses. Columbia Gulf is

committed to responsible operations that protect environmental resources and the health and well-

being of all communities.

        Given the Project’s demonstrated need, reliability benefit, and limited and mitigated

impacts, the public benefits of the Project clearly outweigh any potential effects. Accordingly, the

Project satisfies this element of the Commission’s Certificate Policy Statement.

    D. The Project is Required by the Public Convenience and Necessity

        In summary, the Project is consistent with and required by the public convenience and

necessity. The Project is fully subscribed under a long-term precedent agreement with EKPC

which has committed to 100% of the Project’s capacity. This commitment demonstrates substantial

market support for the Project and will enable EKPC to meet Kentucky’s growing demand for

electricity while enhancing the reliability of the state’s electric grid.

        The Project satisfies the Commission's Certificate Policy Statement because: (i) it is

supported by substantial market demand; (ii) existing customers will not subsidize the Project; (iii)

the Project will not adversely affect existing customers or competing pipelines; (iv) impacts to

landowners, communities, and environmental resources have been avoided and minimized to the

maximum extent practicable; and (v) the public benefits associated with the Project substantially

outweigh any residual adverse effects.




                                                   18
        Accordingly, Columbia Gulf respectfully submits that the Project is required by the present

and future public convenience and necessity and should be approved pursuant to Section 7(c) of

the NGA.

                          1.0     GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION
        This resource report provides general information regarding the proposed Clark Project
(Project), including Project mapping, descriptions of the Project facilities, construction and
restoration methods, applicable permits, and an anticipated construction schedule.

1.1     PROJECT DESCRIPTION
        Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC (Columbia Gulf) has filed an Application for a Certificate
of Public Convenience and Necessity (Application) under Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act, as
amended, with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) for
authorization to construct, operate, and maintain its Clark Project in Estill and Clark counties,
Kentucky. The Project involves the following:

        •   installation of 8.68 miles of new 30-inch diameter greenfield natural gas pipeline
            beginning in Estill County, Kentucky and terminating in Clark County, Kentucky;
        •   construction of a proposed tie-in to the Columbia Gulf Mainline in Estill County,
            Kentucky (hereinafter referred to as the Tie-In Facility), including the installation of a
            new 36-inch by 30-inch bidirectional pig launcher/receiver;
        •   construction and operation of a new meter station designated as the Clark Point of
            Delivery (POD) Meter Station in Clark County, Kentucky (hereinafter referred to as the
            Clark POD), for delivery of natural gas to East Kentucky Power Cooperative’s
            (EKPC’s) J.K. Smith Power Station (Smith Station), and installation of a new 36-inch
            by 30-inch bidirectional pig launcher/receiver; and
        •   usage of online and offline staging areas associated with pipeline construction
            activities in Clark and Rowan counties, Kentucky.

        Pending receipt of all necessary regulatory approvals, Columbia Gulf proposes to begin
construction activities for the Project by September 2027, in order to safely construct and meet a
planned contractual in-service date of August 1, 2028. The Project schedule is further detailed in
Section 1.3.1.

1.1.1   Purpose and Need
        The Project is being developed in response to the Project Shipper’s (EKPC’s) request for
long-term firm natural gas transportation capacity to service its Smith Station located in Clark
County, Kentucky.

        Upon completion, the Project will have the ability to provide up to 250,000 dekatherms per
day (Dth/d) of firm natural gas transportation capacity to the Smith Station, as well as serving as

                                                 1-1
 CLARK PROJECT                                              RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

key infrastructure that will strengthen the reliability and flexibility of Kentucky’s power grid, support
regional economic development and support the growing demands on its system, including the
growing demands of Kentucky’s power-generation customers.

         Columbia Gulf held a Project open season from September 14, 2026, to September 18,
2026, through which it offered firm transportation service for all capacity created by the Project.
At the conclusion of the open season, no other bids were received, and Columbia Gulf entered
into a 20-year precedent agreement with EKPC for 100 percent of the 250,000 Dth/d to be
supplied by the Project.

1.1.2    Location and Description of Facilities
         Columbia Gulf proposes to construct the facilities as summarized in Table 1.1-1 and
depicted in Figure 1.1-1 and Appendix 1A.

Pipeline Facilities

       The Project consists of one new 30-inch diameter greenfield natural gas pipeline, totaling
8.68 miles in length, beginning at the proposed Tie-In Facility in Estill County, Kentucky, and
terminating at the proposed Clark POD in Clark County, Kentucky.                  The two new Project
aboveground facilities are discussed in the aboveground facilities section below.

                                              Table 1.1-2
                                Locations of Co-located Utility Corridors
                       Right-of-Way      Beginning         Ending       Length        Corresponding
      Company

   Eastern Kentucky      Overhead

  Power Co-operative    Power Line
                         Total Co-location                               0.11                --

       Less than one percent (0.11 mile) of the new pipeline will be co-located along existing
EKPC right-of-way (ROW). Table 1.1-2 provides the location of one existing corridor where the
Project is proposed to be co-located. An effort was made to co-locate the new pipeline to existing
utility corridors where possible; however, in the Clark Project vicinity, there are minimal existing
utility corridors present. Additionally, co-location is not feasible in all areas due to residential and
commercial developments, landowner requests, sensitive environmental areas, and/or due to
constructability issues (e.g., crossings of waterbodies, steep slopes, etc.).

Aboveground Facilities

       Aboveground facilities associated with the Project include the Tie-In Facility and the Clark
POD, as further described in the following sections and summarized in Table 1.1-1.

       Tie-In Facility

       Columbia Gulf proposes to install the Tie-In Facility in Estill County, Kentucky, to connect
the existing Columbia Gulf Transmission Mainline 100, Columbia Gulf Transmission Mainline 200,
and Columbia Gulf Transmission Mainline 300 to the new 30-inch pipeline at milepost (MP) 0.00,
as presented in Table 1.1-1. Additionally, the Tie-In Facility will include the installation of a new
36-inch by 30-inch bidirectional pig launcher/receiver within the facility to facilitate in-line
inspections and ensure the integrity of the new pipeline. The new Tie-In Facility will be graveled
and fenced for operational use.

       Clark POD

       Columbia Gulf proposes to install the Clark POD, at the terminus of the new pipeline in
Clark County, Kentucky. The new meter station will connect the new pipeline to EKPC’s Smith

                                                     1-4
 CLARK PROJECT                                                    RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

Station located north of the proposed facility fence line. The Clark POD will also include a new
36-inch by 30-inch bidirectional pig launcher/receiver within the facility fence line to facilitate in-
line inspections and ensure the integrity of the pipeline. The new Clark POD will be graveled and
fenced for operational use. A plot plan depicting the proposed facilities at the Clark POD is
provided in Appendix 1B (provided under separate cover and marked as Critical Energy
Infrastructure Information [CUI//CEII] – Do Not Release).

1.2      LAND REQUIREMENTS
         The Project will require the use of 213.32 acres of land during construction, inclusive of
54.41 acres that will be permanently utilized during operation. A summary of land requirements
for the Project is presented in Table 1.2-1. A detailed description of the land use associated with
the construction and operation of the proposed Project is provided in Resource Report 8 – Land
Use, Recreation, and Aesthetics.

1.2.1    Pipeline Facilities

New Pipeline Right-of-Way

         A 110-foot-wide total construction ROW is necessary for installation of the new 30-inch
pipeline. In general, the construction ROW will be split into an 80-foot working side and a 30-foot
spoil storage side. Where the construction ROW crosses through wetlands, the typical corridor
width will be reduced to 75 feet, with the construction ROW split between a 50-foot working side

                                                           1-5
 CLARK PROJECT                                           RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

and a 25-foot spoil side. A 50-foot permanent ROW will be maintained for operations of the new
pipeline. Some portions of the 50-foot permanent ROW may overlap with existing ROWs where
co-located, as presented in Table 1.1-2. The proposed ROW width of the new pipeline is depicted
in the construction typicals provided in Appendix 1B.

       The total acreage of land that will be affected by construction of the new pipeline (not
including additional temporary workspace [ATWS], contractor/staging/pipe yards, and access
roads) will total 112.15 acres. As referenced above, in order to minimize new impacts associated

1.3.2   General Construction Procedures

Surveying and Staking

        A crew will stake the outside limits of the proposed construction corridor and ATWS, the
centerline of the pipeline and drainages, highway crossings, and access roads.                Affected
landowners will be notified prior to pre-construction staking. Existing utility lines (e.g., cables,
conduits, and pipelines) will be located and marked with flags, stakes, or other devices to prevent
accidental damage during construction.        Previously identified sensitive resources, such as
waterbody and wetland boundaries, will also be located and marked to minimize or avoid adverse
impacts during construction.

Clearing and Grading

        Following the establishment of workspace boundaries, the Project workspace will be
cleared of vegetation and debris, where necessary. The construction corridor will be graded,
where necessary, to create a level workspace to allow safe passage of equipment. Grading will
be limited in wetland areas. Large obstacles, such as trees, rocks, brush, and logs will be moved,
and the natural drainage will be preserved to the extent practicable. Columbia Gulf will implement
soil mitigation procedures as outlined in the FERC Plan immediately following clearing, with the
exception of areas in which vegetation is cut by hand, and throughout grading activities. Cleared
timber, vegetation, and debris along the construction corridor will be disposed of on-site (e.g.,
chipped and spread, burned) or disposed of at an approved off-site location in accordance with
federal and state regulations.

        Fences will be cut and braced along the construction corridor and temporary gates will be
installed as necessary to control livestock and limit public access. In unsaturated wetlands,
agricultural, and residential areas, conserved topsoil will be stockpiled, typically along one side of
the construction ROW, allowing the other side to be used for access, material transport, and pipe
assembly. In agricultural areas where topsoil is stripped from the entire construction corridor,
ATWS may be used for topsoil storage. A maximum of 12 inches of topsoil will typically be
removed or stripped and segregated in these areas. If the topsoil is less than 12 inches in depth,
the actual depth of the topsoil will be removed and segregated.

Trenching

        Trenching involves excavation of a ditch for pipeline placement and is accomplished
through the use of a rotary trenching machine, track-mounted backhoe, or similar equipment.

Typically, the width of the trench will be cut at least 12 inches wider than the width of the pipe.
Each trench will be excavated between 6- to 10-feet-deep to allow for a minimum 3 feet of cover
between the top of the pipe and the final land surface after backfilling, as required by 49 CFR 192.
The width at the top of the trench will vary to allow the side slopes to be adapted to local conditions
at the time of construction and will range from 10 to 15 feet in areas where construction personnel
will not be required to work in the trench.

       Columbia Gulf will employ best management practices outlined in the FERC Plan and
Procedures to minimize erosion during trenching operations and construction activities. Where
necessary, temporary and permanent erosion control devices (ECDs) will be installed and
maintained to contain disturbed soils during trenching in uplands and to minimize potential erosion
and sedimentation of wetlands and waterbodies.

Pipe Stringing, Bending, and Welding

       Steel pipe will be protected with an epoxy coating applied at the factory (the beveled ends
will be left uncoated for welding) and shipped to the staging areas or strung directly onto the
construction corridor.    The individual or pre-assembled joints will be transported to the
construction corridor and placed along the trench line in a single line to allow welding operations
to proceed efficiently.

       Once placed on the construction corridor, some bending of the pipe will be required to
allow the pipeline to follow natural grade changes and direction changes. Typically, joints will be
field bent by track-mounted hydraulic bending machines, as necessary, prior to line-up and
welding. For larger horizontal changes of direction, manufactured induction bends or fittings will
be used. Only welders qualified according to applicable American National Standards Institute,
American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and American Petroleum Institute will be permitted
to perform the welding. To ensure that the assembled pipe will meet or exceed the design
strength requirements, the welds will be visually inspected and non-destructively tested using
radiographic (x-ray) or other approved test method, in accordance with American Petroleum
Institute standards. Welds displaying inclusions (void spaces) or other defects will be repaired or
cut out (removed), and the new or repaired weld will be installed and retested.

       Following welding, the previously uncoated ends of the pipe at the joints will be epoxy
coated. Prior to lowering the assembled pipe into the trench, the coating on the entire pipe section
will be inspected and any damaged areas will be repaired.

Pipe Lowering

       The completed sections of assembled pipe will be lifted off temporary supports and
lowered into the trench(es) by side-boom tractors, or other equipment. Before lowering the pipe,
the trench will be inspected to ensure that it is free of rock and other debris that could damage
the pipe or the coating. In addition, the pipe and trench will be visually inspected to ensure that
the pipe and trench configurations are compatible. Tie-in welding and pipe coating between pipe
strings will occur within the excavated bell-hole trench to join the newly lowered-in section with
the previously installed sections of pipe.

Padding and Backfilling

       After the pipe is lowered into the trench, the trench will be backfilled in accordance with
the FERC Plan. Previously excavated materials will be placed back into the trench using bladed
equipment or backhoes. Where the previously excavated material contains large rocks or other
materials that could damage the pipe or coating, clean fill will be placed around the pipe prior to
backfilling. Any excess excavated materials or materials unsuitable for backfill will be spread
evenly over the construction work area or transported off-site for proper disposal. The trench will
be backfilled to grade or above its original elevation (i.e., slightly crowned) to accommodate any
subsequent settling.

Hydrostatic Testing

       Following the backfilling of the trench, the new pipeline will be cleaned and hydrostatically
tested to ensure that the system is free from leaks and is capable of operating at the proposed
operating pressure. Upon filling the pipe, water will be pressurized and held in accordance with
USDOT regulations (49 CFR Part 192). Any loss of pressure that cannot be attributed to other
factors, such as temperature changes, will be investigated. Any leaks detected will be repaired
and the segments that are repaired will be retested. Upon completion of the testing, the water
will be discharged in well-vegetated upland areas, in accordance with applicable federal and state
regulations. Hydrostatic test water will only be in contact with new steel pipe or frac tanks that
will be free of chemicals or lubricants. Once a segment of pipe has been successfully tested and
dried, the test cap and manifold will be removed, and the pipe will be connected to the remainder
of the piping. Hydrostatic testing is further discussed in Resource Report 2 – Water Use and
Quality. The necessary permits associated with hydrostatic testing for the Project are identified
in Table 1.6-1.

1.3.3   Specialized Construction Techniques
        In addition to conventional pipeline construction activities, specialized construction
techniques will be utilized in sensitive resource areas including waterbody crossings, wetland
crossings, residential areas, agricultural areas, road crossings, areas requiring reduced
workspace, and across karst terrain. Specialized construction procedures are described below.

Waterbody Crossings

        Construction methods utilized at waterbody crossings are highly dependent on the
characteristics of the waterbody encountered at the time of construction. Waterbody crossing
methods anticipated to be used during construction of the Project include conventional open-cut
and conventional bore, as described below.         The proposed construction method for each
waterbody crossed by the Project is identified in Resource Report 2, Appendix 2B.

                                                1-15
 CLARK PROJECT                                          RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

       Open-Cut

       Waterbodies less than 100 feet wide will typically be crossed via the conventional open-
cut method. The open-cut crossing method employs the same general construction procedures
that were described above for mainline construction. Equipment will operate from the banks of
the waterbody to the maximum extent practicable to excavate a trench. As required by the FERC
Procedures, flow will be maintained at all times. Excavated material from the trench will be placed
on the bank above the ordinary high-water mark for use as backfill. The pipe segment will be
prefabricated and weighted, as necessary, to provide negative buoyancy. Columbia Gulf will
install the pipeline with a minimum of 6 feet of cover unless otherwise required by applicable
federal, state, or local permits. Typical backfill cover requirements will be met, contours will be
restored within the waterbody, and the banks will be stabilized via seeding and the installation of
erosion control matting. A detailed description of the potential impacts on waterbodies and water
quality, as well as the measures that Columbia Gulf will implement to minimize these impacts, is
provided in Resource Report 2. A depiction of typical conventional open-cut waterbody crossing
construction techniques is provided in Appendix 1B.

       Flume

       The flume crossing method is an alternative to the open-cut method in which water flow is
temporarily directed through one or more flume pipes placed over the excavation area.
Temporary dams (consisting of sandbags, bladders, or other impervious materials) are installed
upstream and downstream of the proposed crossing and are used to divert water into the flume(s).
The use of the flume allows trenching and pipeline installation to occur primarily under dry
conditions without significant disruption of water flow.

       Dam and Pump

       The dam and pump crossing method is similar to the flume crossing method in that it is an
alternative to the open-cut method that allows trenching and pipeline installation to occur under
relatively dry conditions with minimal impact to water flow. This method involves the temporary
installation of dams (consisting of sandbags, bladders, or other impervious materials) upstream
and downstream of the proposed crossing. Pumps are then used to dewater the excavation area
and to transport the water flow around the construction work area.

        Horizontal Directional Drill

        The HDD crossing method is typically utilized at large or sensitive waterbody or wetland
crossings and certain road crossings.       The HDD method allows for installation beneath a
waterbody, wetland, or road without the excavation of a trench by drilling a hole below
conventional pipeline depth and pulling the pipeline through the pre-drilled hole. One HDD
crossing has been identified for the Project and will be utilized to avoid trenching impacts on the
Red River from MPs 4.01 to 4.40, for a total of 2,013 feet. The plan and profile drawing for the
proposed HDD crossing is provided in Appendix 1B.

Wetland Crossings

        The construction ROW width will be limited to 75 feet in wetlands per the FERC
Procedures, unless otherwise requested and approved, and buffers will be clearly marked during
construction activities.

        Operation of construction equipment through wetlands will be limited to only that
necessary for each stage of pipe installation (e.g., clearing, trenching, etc.), all other equipment
and vehicles will cross through the wetland on a matted crossing. Topsoil segregation techniques
in accordance with the FERC Procedures will be utilized in unsaturated wetlands to preserve the
seed bank and allow for successful restoration of the disturbed area following completion of
Project activities. Disturbed wetlands will be monitored post-construction to ensure successful
revegetation. To further minimize impacts to wetlands, refueling will not be conducted, and fuel
will not be stored, within 100 feet of wetlands.

        Wetland crossings for the Project will be accomplished via the open-cut method, similarly,
as described above. However, Columbia Gulf will install the pipeline with a minimum of 4 feet of
cover unless otherwise required by applicable federal, state, or local permits.

        Per the FERC Procedures, Columbia Gulf will not utilize topsoil segregation techniques in
inundated wetlands. Wetlands to be crossed by the Project, as well as detailed descriptions of
potential impacts and Columbia Gulf’s proposed mitigation measures to minimize these impacts,
are further described in Resource Report 2. A depiction of typical wetland construction techniques
is provided in Appendix 1B.

Road and Utility Crossings

       Open-Cut

       Generally, pipeline crossings of lightly traveled and unimproved rural dirt or gravel roads
will typically be accomplished using the open-cut installation method, as described above. The
trench for an open-cut crossing is excavated with a backhoe or similar equipment, all backfill is
compacted, and the road is resurfaced.          If open-cut road construction requires extensive
construction time, provisions will be made for detours or other measures to permit traffic flow
during construction.

       Conventional Bore Method

       Certain roads, highways, and utilities will be crossed using conventional bore
methodology, similar to the method described above. The bore method involves the excavation
of pits on either side of the transportation feature and the placement of a bore machine within one
of the pits. This device will bore under the road and install the pipeline segment. Once the bore
has reached the other pit, the pipeline segment will be tied in with the pipeline installed on the
other side. With this method, the pipeline would pass under the roadway, highway, or utility with
little or no disturbance to traffic along the roadway.

control measures are established.

 CLARK PROJECT                                          RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

        Although side slope terrain has been reduced to the maximum extent practicable during
routing, side slopes will still be encountered. In such areas of side slope terrain, the upslope side
of the construction corridor will be cut during grading. The material removed from the cut will be
used to fill the downslope edge of the construction corridor to provide a safe and level surface
from which to operate the heavy equipment. As such, ATWS may be required downslope of side
slope terrain to accommodate the fill material. During grade restoration, the spoil will be placed
back in the cut and compacted to restore original contours.

        There is a relatively low potential for subsurface karst features to present in the Project
area (see Resource Report 6 for further discussion). Columbia Gulf has developed a Karst
Mitigation Plan that details specific construction, restoration, and mitigation measures that
Columbia Gulf will implement to address karst features if encountered during construction
(Appendix 1B).

Blasting

        Blasting may be required to excavate the trench in areas where rock is encountered at
depths that interfere with conventional excavation or rock-trenching methods. If blasting is
deemed necessary, a licensed subcontractor will be hired to conduct the blasting operations.
Columbia Gulf has developed a Blasting Plan that establishes procedures and safety measures
that Columbia Gulf will implement during construction (Appendix 1B).                In addition, the
subcontractor would utilize seismically-monitored blasting techniques in compliance with federal
and state regulations and include applicable mitigation measures such as the placement of
blasting mats as appropriate.

        Per the FERC Procedures, prior to blasting, the final Blasting Plan and schedule will be
submitted to FERC for notification should blasting occur within any waterbody identified as habitat
for federally listed threatened or endangered species. Blasting is further discussed in Resource
Report 6.

1.3.4   Aboveground Facility Construction Procedures
        Landowner notification, surveying, and staking of the Project areas associated with the
Project aboveground facilities will be conducted using the same general procedures described
above in Section 1.3.2 for the pipeline facilities. Aboveground and belowground piping will be
installed and hydrostatically tested prior to placing in-service. Additionally, safety and control
devices will be installed and tested prior to operation. The placement of gravel within the facility
fence line will begin with grading, leveling, and compacting the soils. Fencing will then be


                                                1-20
 CLARK PROJECT                                         RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

constructed around the new facilities. Once construction is complete, all disturbed areas not
covered with gravel will be graded, restored, and reseeded in accordance with the FERC Plan
and Procedures.

1.3.5   Proposed Site-Specific Modifications to the FERC Plan and Procedures
        Columbia Gulf is committed to constructing the Project in accordance with the FERC Plan
and Procedures to the extent feasible. However, there are locations where topography, existing
infrastructure, and/or natural conditions make it impractical to implement some of the measures
specified in these documents. Appendix 1D presents the site-specific deviations to the FERC
Plan and Procedures identified to date and includes the justification for why the deviations are
necessary as well any proposed equal compliance measures.

1.3.6   Environmental Compliance, Training, and Inspection
        Columbia Gulf will include, whenever possible, implementation details in its construction
drawings and specifications to ensure that the construction of the proposed facilities will comply
with the FERC Certificate conditions, mitigation measures identified in the resource reports and
requirements of other federal and state permitting agencies. Columbia Gulf’s selected contractors
will receive copies of the design specifications, FERC Plan and Procedures, and other
environmental documents.

        For mitigation measures that address pre-construction surveys and clearances, Columbia
Gulf will provide pertinent correspondence and documentation to the contractor(s). For those
mitigation measures that address permit conditions from federal and state agencies, Columbia
Gulf will provide copies of permits and related drawings. For those mitigation measures that, in
part, address post-construction requirements, Columbia Gulf’s engineers will provide instructions
and documentation to Columbia Gulf’s operating personnel following the completion of
construction. Columbia Gulf will require selected contractors to install facilities according to
Columbia Gulf and USDOT specifications, specific permit conditions, and the terms of their
construction contracts with Columbia Gulf.

Training

        Columbia Gulf will conduct environmental training for its field personnel and the
construction contractor personnel regarding proper field implementation of the FERC Plan and
Procedures, other site-specific environmental documents, regulatory conditions, and other
mitigation measures. Columbia Gulf will provide copies of permits and related drawings to



                                               1-21
 CLARK PROJECT                                         RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

contractor supervisory personnel prior to the start of construction and ensure that all entities
understand the proper procedures for construction, stabilization, and restoration.

Inspectors and Compliance Responsibility

       For purposes of quality assurance and compliance with mitigation measures, applicable
regulatory requirements, and Columbia Gulf specifications, Columbia Gulf will be represented by
at least one environmental inspector (EI) to oversee and document environmental compliance at
all proposed facilities for the Project, and prepare the regular construction status reports, as
directed by FERC throughout construction. Columbia Gulf will also require the prime contractor
to assign at least one environmental foreman (i.e., environmental compliance specialist) for the
Project. The environmental foreman will be responsible for overseeing the successful installation
and maintenance of ECDs by the prime contractor and implementation of suitable mitigation
measures for construction in environmentally sensitive areas.

       The EI(s) will report directly to Columbia Gulf’s Environmental Compliance Manager, will
coordinate with the Chief Inspector, and will have stop-work authority. The EIs’ duties will be
consistent with those contained in paragraph II.B (Responsibilities of Environmental Inspectors)
of the FERC Plan and will include ensuring compliance with environmental conditions from the
FERC Certificate, Columbia Gulf’s environmental designs and specifications, and other permits
or authorizations.   The construction drawing package will be distributed to Columbia Gulf’s
inspectors and to contractor supervisory personnel. If contractor performance is unsatisfactory,
the contract terms will allow Columbia Gulf to stop work in progress and cause a contractor to
begin remedial work.

       Columbia Gulf’s engineering and construction departments are responsible for designing
and constructing certificated facilities in compliance with regulatory and non-regulatory
requirements and agreements. Any issues of non-compliance with mitigation measures or other
regulatory requirements that cannot be solved in the field will be addressed by the Columbia Gulf
Project Manager and the Columbia Gulf Environmental Compliance and Permitting Managers.
Routine reporting or specific communication with the FERC staff regarding design, installation,
and maintenance of the facilities will be the responsibility of Columbia Gulf’s Environmental
Permitting Department.    FERC staff inquiries regarding these proposed facilities should be
addressed to Columbia Gulf’s Environmental Planning and Permitting Department accordingly.




                                               1-22
 CLARK PROJECT                                          RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

1.4     OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE
        Columbia Gulf will operate and maintain the newly constructed Project facilities in the
same manner as it currently operates and maintains its existing system and in accordance with
the requirements of FERC and USDOT’s regulations, set forth in 49 CFR 192, pursuant to the
provisions of the Natural Gas Pipeline Safety Act of 1968, as amended, and industry-proven
practices and techniques. It is anticipated that following the completion of construction, operation
of the Project will be assigned to existing operations resources. The proposed pipeline and
aboveground facilities will be patrolled on a routine basis, and personnel well-qualified to perform
both routine and non-routine maintenance on pipeline facilities will handle all maintenance.

        The following sections provide specific details on standard operating and maintenance
procedures for aboveground facilities and permanent easement areas, including erosion control
procedures and periodic pipeline ROW patrols.

1.4.1   Pipeline Facilities
        During periodic pipeline ROW patrols, attention will be given to conditions that could
damage the pipeline or create unsafe operating conditions, such as unauthorized encroachment
or other activities in the vicinity of the ROW. The local operations supervisor will be notified of
any conditions requiring attention, and corrective measures will be performed, as needed.

        Maintenance of the permanent pipeline ROW will include periodic mowing as necessary,
in accordance with the FERC Plan to allow for visual inspections. Actively cultivated areas will
be allowed to revert to pre-construction use for the full width of the ROW. In all other upland
areas, a 50-foot-wide permanent pipeline ROW will continue to be maintained in a primarily
herbaceous state in accordance with the FERC Plan.

        The new pipeline and associated facilities will comply with Pipeline and Hazardous
Materials Safety Administration requirements regarding markers. Columbia Gulf participates in
One-Call systems.

1.4.2   Aboveground Facilities
        Columbia Gulf’s personnel will perform routine checks of the Project facilities, including
calibration of equipment and instrumentation, inspection of critical components, and scheduled
and routine maintenance of equipment and grounds. At the Project aboveground facilities,
vegetation with the fenced area will be mowed and/or herbicides applied, as needed. Herbicide
treatments will be in accordance with the FERC Plan and manufacturer recommendations, as well



                                                1-23
 CLARK PROJECT                                                RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

as state and federal regulations. Operational testing will be performed on safety equipment to
ensure proper function. Corrective actions will be taken as necessary if issues are identified.

1.5       FUTURE PLANS AND ABANDONMENT
          Because Columbia Gulf is a provider of natural gas transportation, it must remain
responsive to its customers’ needs for pipeline capacity. Hence, Columbia Gulf is constantly
evaluating its customers’ needs and whether or not such needs can be met by existing
infrastructure or whether additional facilities are required. Market forces will determine the timing
and need for future expansions or abandonment and would be filed as such under a separate
docket.

          TC Energy and its subsidiaries, including Columbia Gulf, have not identified any additional
plans for future expansion or abandonment of the Project facilities described in this resource
report. However, demand for pipeline capacity is dynamic and making long-term predictions is
speculative at best. Columbia Gulf will continue to work with market participants to develop
expansions across its natural gas transmission systems to meet the demands of the market. If
additional demand for natural gas requires future expansion, Columbia Gulf will seek the
appropriate authorizations from FERC. When and if an application is filed, the environmental
impact of the new proposed facilities would be examined.

1.6       PERMITS AND APPROVALS
          Federal, state, and local permits, authorizations, or clearances, as applicable, for the
construction of the Project are identified in Table 1.6-1. Agency correspondence and consultation
records are provided in Appendix 1C. Contact information for federal, state, and local permitting
agencies is provided in Appendix 1E.

1.6.1   Stakeholder Outreach
        Columbia Gulf initiated public outreach to stakeholders for the Project beginning in March
2025. Efforts have been made to inform the public, particularly landowners and local, state, and
federal officials, about the proposed Project, including personal visits, phone calls, emails, and
written correspondence. In addition, Columbia Gulf will hold an open house in the Project vicinity
on November 10, 2026. Columbia Gulf looks forward to discussing the following topics at the
open house, including landowner and property rights, how to support the Project, environmental,
construction and contractor questions, community involvement opportunities, engineering, routing
and design, and protocols in the event of an incident, among others.                      The objective in
implementing a comprehensive stakeholder outreach strategy is to identify and potentially resolve
issues raised by stakeholders in a timely fashion. Columbia Gulf will work cooperatively with all
affected landowners and stakeholders to attempt to address any concerns and to minimize, to the
extent practicable, any adverse impacts that may arise. A Project stakeholder list is provided in
Appendix 1E.

1.6.2   Landowner Notification
        Columbia Gulf originally began talking to landowners about the Project in March 2025.
Columbia Gulf’s land agents provided the landowners with a business card that has the agent’s

                                                       1-25
 CLARK PROJECT                                           RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

email and Columbia Gulf’s landowner hotline. The agent has and will continue to maintain contact
with the landowners through the acquisition, construction and restoration phase. Furthermore,
agents will be available in the field to address landowner concerns as they arise. Additionally,
Columbia Gulf will provide Project fact sheets to all affected landowners and stakeholders
including local, state, and government officials to introduce them to the Project. Each mailing
contains a description of the Project and a map depicting the location of the existing and proposed
facilities, the Project’s toll-free telephone number and the website, which went live in October
2026, where stakeholders can obtain additional information about the Project. The names and
addresses of landowners whose property will be directly affected by or about the Project facilities
or work areas are provided in Appendix 1F (provided under separate cover and marked as
Privileged and Confidential Information (CUI//PRIV) – Do Not Release).

       Pursuant to 18 CFR 157.6(d) of the Commission’s regulations, Columbia Gulf will notify
all owners of properties that are directly affected by the proposed construction activities and
abutting the proposed construction activities within three days of the Commission issuing its
Notice of Application for the Project and provide information regarding procedures to follow in the
event that a landowner has any concerns or problems during construction. Columbia Gulf will
also publish a public notice of the Application filing twice in a daily or weekly newspaper of general
circulation in the Project counties within 14 days of the Commission issuing its Notice of
Application for the Project. Written notices will be published in the Estill County Tribune and the
Winchester Sun newspapers local to the Project vicinity.

       Columbia Gulf will also place complete copies of the Application at the following central
locations in the Project area:

       •   Clark County Public Library
           370 South Burns Ave.
           Winchester, KY 40391
       •   Estill County Public Library
           184 Broadway Street
           Irvine, KY 40336

       Throughout the course of the Project, landowners and other concerned citizens will be
kept informed about Project permitting developments, construction, and restoration through
various means, such as Project notification letters and the Project website, located at:

       https://www.tcenergy.com/operations/natural-gas/clark-project
