 CLARK PROJECT                                            RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

1.7     NON-JURISDICTIONAL FACILITIES
        Non-jurisdictional facilities are those facilities related to the Project that are constructed,
owned, and operated by others that are not subject to FERC jurisdiction.                 At this time,
non-jurisdictional facilities necessary to operate the Project are anticipated to include minor
facilities and drops necessary to provide power to the bidirectional pig launcher/receiver at the
Tie-In Facility and the Clark POD. The electricity for the Clark POD will come from a 120/240 Volt
power line and will be installed by the Clark Energy Cooperative in 2028.

        In accordance with Section 380.12(c)(2)(ii) of the FERC regulations, Columbia Gulf has
conducted an evaluation to determine the potential need for FERC to conduct an environmental
review of the Project-related non-jurisdictional facilities.     Columbia Gulf has established the
facilities associated with the Project in accordance with proposed and existing points of
connection with its existing pipeline system; therefore, the non-jurisdictional facilities have had no
effect on the location or configuration of the Project facilities.

        The non-jurisdictional facilities are part of private construction projects under state and
local jurisdiction. The federal government has no financial involvement, and no federal lands are
involved; therefore, there is no cumulative federal control or responsibility associated with these
facilities. Additionally, FERC has no authority over the permitting, licensing, funding, construction,
or operation of local electric lines, thus FERC is not required to perform an environmental review
of the non-jurisdictional facilities discussed herein.       However, potential cumulative impacts
associated with construction of the non-jurisdictional electrical facilities are discussed in each of
the applicable resource reports.

1.8     CUMULATIVE IMPACTS
        The potential cumulative impacts associated with the Project may result from impacts
associated with construction and operation of the Project facilities combined with the impacts from
non-jurisdictional facilities as well as other proposed major developments occurring within the
vicinity of the Project. To review potential cumulative impacts, Columbia Gulf considered projects
that will be completed within one year prior to the start of construction, as well as present and
reasonably foreseeable future major projects including infrastructure projects, pipelines,
commercial and residential developments, and large industrial projects within the Project area.
Columbia Gulf also considered potential cumulative impacts associated with its other concurrent
projects including projects that will be completed within one year prior to the start of construction
or proposed projects with a definitive project scope.



                                                  1-27
 CLARK PROJECT                                                 RESOURCE REPORT 1 – GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

        The Council on Environmental Quality’s Cumulative Effects Guidance states that certain
“future actions can be excluded from the analysis of cumulative effects if the action is outside the
geographic boundaries or time frame established for the cumulative effects analysis; the action
will not affect resources that are the subject of the cumulative effects analysis; or including the
action would be arbitrary” (Council on Environmental Quality, 1997).

        Based on these criteria, Columbia Gulf has determined that for an action to be included in
this cumulative impact assessment, it must:

        •    Impact a resource potentially affected by the Project,
        •    Cause this impact within all, or part of, the geographic scope, and
        •    Cause this impact within all, or part of, the timeframe in which the Project will have an
             impact.

        For the cumulative impacts analysis, focus was placed on resources identified within the
resource reports including groundwater; surface water; vegetation and wildlife (primarily
threatened and endangered species); cultural resources; geology and soils; land use, recreation,
and aesthetics; and air and noise quality. The geographic scopes differ by resource and are
further defined below in Table 1.8-1.
